title: Research method for multi-ancestry proteome-phenome-wide atlas
bodyHtml:
A brief overview of the methods used to generate the protein-phenotype results on the Knowledge portal interface is provided (see Figure 1). More details can be found in the original paper.

Figure 1. An overview of the analyses performed.

1. Proteomics cohorts

We analyzed proteomics cohorts from three ancestries consisting of European (four cohorts: ARIC, deCODE, Fenland, and UKB-PPP), African (two cohorts: ARIC and UKB-PPP), and East Asian (one cohort: Kyoto University Nagahama East Asian cohort). All cohorts had proteomics measurements from the aptamer-based SomaScan assay v4 from SomaLogic (Boulder, Colorado, USA) aside from the UKB-PPP study had proteomics measurements from the antibody-based Olink Explore 3072 platform. 

2. Strict variant-to-gene (v2g) cis-protein quantitative trait loci (pQTLs)

We performed linkage disequilibrium (LD) clumping (clumping window of 1 Mb, P < 5 × 10−8, and clumping r2 threshold of 0.001) on each proteomics GWAS in each ancestry cohort to identify independent loci. Genetic instruments for MR were derived from a unique strict variant-to-gene (V2G) definition for cis-pQTLs whereby a cis-pQTL is a strict V2G cis-pQTL if it is a cis-pQTL for only one protein-coding gene (strict) and it has the strongest link to the corresponding protein-coding gene based on multiple sources of evidence and concomitantly has the highest Open Targets Genetics V2G score (Figure 2).

Figure 2. Strict V2G cis-pQTLs.

3. GWAS outcomes

We manually curated the latest and largest GWAS (as of February 2024) for 179 European and 26 African ancestry outcomes. For East Asian ancestry outcomes, we selected 206 outcomes from BioBank Japan. See Figure 3a and Figure 3b.

Figure 3. (a) GWAS outcomes, (b) phenotype categories of the GWAS outcomes, (c) MR and colocalization analyses flow chart.

4. Two-sample Mendelian randomization 

To mitigate horizontal pleiotropy, we used strict V2G cis-pQTLs as instrumental variables to proxy protein-level exposures. We harmonized exposure and outcome GWAS and performed a proxy search if an instrument was absent in the outcome GWAS. For proteins with a single genetic instrument, the association between the protein and outcome was evaluated using a Wald ratio estimate. For proteins with two or more genetic instruments, the association was assessed using an inverse variance weighted random effects estimate. We corrected for multiple testing per cohort in each ancestry by applying a Benjamini-Hochberg-corrected P threshold (false discovery rate, FDR) of 0.05 (5%).

4.1. MR sensitivity analyses

We further filtered MR results based on multiple sensitivity analyses, including heterogeneity tests, MR using alternative approaches (including weighted median, weighted mode, MR-Egger), and Steiger directionality test to assess reverse causality. Following these filtering steps, we termed retained protein-phenotype associations “MR-passing”. The sensitivity analyses are described for proteins with two or more instruments and proteins with three or more instruments below:

4.1.1. Sensitivity analyses for proteins with two or more instruments

The heterogeneity test was performed for proteins with two or more instruments and describes whether strict variant-to-gene cis-pQTLs of the same protein are likely to show comparable effects on the tested outcomes. For heterogeneity testing, we computed a heterogeneity P value (Q_pval)  and we calculated I2 ­statistics. If an association had an I2 threshold ≥ 0.5 and a heterogeneity P value (Q_pval) < 0.05, this indicated considerable heterogeneity. 

4.1.2. Sensitivity analyses for proteins with three or more instruments

For proteins with three or more genetic instruments, we performed additional sensitivity analyses using alternative MR methods such as MR weighted median, MR weighted mode, and MR-Egger methods, as well as Steiger directionality testing. To check the consistency of MR estimates, we required the MR estimate, as well as the sensitivity analyses estimates from the MR weighted median, MR weighted mode, and MR-Egger approaches, to all have the same sign. For directional pleiotropy, we performed the MR-Egger intercept test and considered a P value < 0.05 as a statistically significant deviation from the null and an indication of directional pleiotropy. We also performed Steiger filtering on all proteins. Any pQTLs that explained more variance in the outcome than in the exposure potentially indicated reverse causation.

5. Colocalization of proteomic GWAS with outcome GWAS

To assess whether plasma protein levels share the same causal variant with GWAS outcomes, we performed PWCoCo and SharePro for MR associations that passed all MR sensitivity analyses described in the previous section. Colocalization analyses were performed around a 1-Mb (±500-kb) region centered on the lead cis-pQTL (lowest P value cis-pQTL). We set a colocalization posterior probability (PP) of a shared causal variant ≥ 0.8 in any of PWCoCo or SharePro as evidence of colocalization. We reported putatively causal associations as associations which pass all MR sensitivity analyses, Steiger filtering, and also colocalized with a PP ≥ 0.8 in any one of PWCoCo or SharePro on the interface (Figure 3c). The interface contains MR and colocalization summaries, summaries of effect direction consistency across cohorts, flags of proteins instrumented by PAVs of high impact (see Note), and whether the protein-phenotype association came from a protein uniquely instrumentable in that ancestry. 

Note: To check whether the strict V2G cis-pQTL was a PAV of high impact, we annotated the variant and all its LD proxies (r2 > 0.8) using Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor. “High” impact variants are disruptive and can cause truncation of proteins, loss of function, or trigger nonsense-mediated decay. If a strict V2G cis-pQTL or any of its LD proxies were labeled as High, we considered this strict V2G cis-pQTL to be a PAV of High impact.
